itens.titulo: Feast of the Holy Guardian Angels
itens.resumo: Liturgical memorial celebrated on October 2, dedicated to the guardian angels, with roots in medieval European devotions and papal institutionalization beginning in the early seventeenth century.
itens.corpo:
Devotion to the guardian angels has ancient roots and gained its own liturgical expression especially from the Middle Ages onward. Before the modern liturgical reforms, local celebrations of the guardian angels are presumed to have existed in various regions of Europe; the Sacro Convento and the Franciscans cultivated it with particular zeal. The Franciscan friar John Colombi composed a proper Office, whose approval is attributed to Leo X (1515). A later devotional narrative even places the beginning of the feast in England in the "year 800"; the more prudent sources, however, place the independent feast in fifteenth-century Spain, from where it spread to Portugal, Austria and the rest of the continent. Originally, the angels were celebrated on September 29, together with the three archangels (Michael, Gabriel and Raphael), so that the differentiation of a memorial of its own responded to the desire to honor in a special way the personal angel of each believer.

The Roman institutionalization came about in successive steps. With the promulgation of the Missal of Saint Pius V (1570), the particular feasts of the guardian angels were removed from the Roman calendar; in 1608, Pope Paul V restored them for some regions. In 1670, Pope Clement X (1670-1676) extended the Memorial of the Holy Guardian Angels to the whole Church of the Roman Rite, fixing it on October 2 — some sources alternatively indicate 1672; the discrepancy remains among authors.

On July 5, 1883, a decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, approved by Pope Leo XIII, raised the feast from the rank of "lesser double" to "greater double," endowing it with its own Mass, first Vespers and Matins with nine lessons, so that it would no longer be omitted when concurring with other celebrations. The text appears in the primary source Acta Sanctae Sedis, vol. 16 (1883), pp. 47-48, and fits within the broader liturgical program of Leo XIII in that period (the encyclical Supremi apostolatus officio on the Rosary dates from September 1, 1883). With the liturgical reform of the Second Vatican Council, the Memorial was retained in the Missal of 1969, keeping a good part of the prayers of the 1962 missal; only the prayer after Communion is newly composed. The proper Preface of the Angels, "Qui mirabili ordinis," reiterates that God governs heaven and earth through the angels.

The doctrine underlying the memorial of October 2 is that God entrusts a guardian angel to each human person. Although it has not been the object of formal dogmatic definition, it is held as the "sense of the Church": Saint Jerome wrote that "the dignity of the soul is so great that each one has, from birth, an angel commissioned to guard it" (Commentary on Matthew, XVIII, book II), and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (no. 336) takes up this doctrine by affirming that, from infancy to death, human life is surrounded by their watchful care and intercession. The Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium (no. 50) recalls the affection due to the "holy Angels" in communion with the heavenly Church. The feast is a traditional occasion to renew personal devotion to one's own guardian angel, and linked to it is the prayer Angele Dei, whose authorship is today attributed to Reginald of Canterbury (died c. 1109).

The association of October 2 with a civil celebration related to grandparents, in Italy in 2005, is a modern development of a non-liturgical character, inspired by the protective figure of the guardian angels, but without the value of worship.

itens.resumo: Name given in the New Testament to Satan as the "prince of demons," derived from an ancient Philistine deity of Ekron and probably distorted by a contemptuous pun.
itens.corpo:
The name Beelzebub (in the Greek of the Gospels, Beelzeboul) goes back to the Hebrew Baal-Zebub, "lord of the flies," the title of a Philistine deity worshiped in the city of Ekron. The Second Book of Kings relates that King Ahaziah, being ill, sends messengers to consult this god instead of the God of Israel; the prophet Elijah intercepts the envoys and announces the king's death as punishment for having sought "a god of Ekron" (2 Kings 1:2-16). In the Septuagint, the name appears explicitly as "Baal-fly, god of Akkaron."

Scholars debate the original meaning of the title. One school reads it literally as "lord of the flies"; another maintains that the original form would have been Baal-Zebul, "lord of the dwelling" or "exalted lord" (from the root zevul, "mansion," "lofty dwelling"), and that Hebrew scribes deliberately distorted it into "lord of the flies" or even "lord of dung," in a mocking pun against the worship of Baal. Rabbinic literature treats the term as a mockery of idolatrous worship. This ambiguity explains why, in the New Testament, the form Beelzeboul circulates chiefly, and not Baal-Zebub.

In the Gospel, the name designates Satan himself as the "prince of demons." The Pharisees accuse Jesus of casting out demons "by the prince of demons" (Mt 12:24; Mk 3:22; Lk 11:15); in Mt 9:34 the same accusation had already appeared. Jesus refutes it with the argument that "every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste" — it would make no sense for Satan to cast out himself — and affirms that he casts out demons "by the finger of God" (Lk 11:20) or "by the Spirit of God" (Mt 12:28), a sign that the Kingdom of God has come. In Mt 10:25 Jesus himself seems to play on the sense of "lord of the house": if they have called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household.

Later spiritual tradition kept Beelzebub as one of the names used to designate the leader of evil in the world. One must not, however, confuse Scripture with a detailed "infernal hierarchy": the Old and New Testaments do not offer an ordered list of demons. Systematic demonology — such as that which, from the sixteenth century on, classified demons by capital vices — is a later theological and folkloric elaboration, popularized by works such as the Dictionnaire Infernal (1818) by Jacques-Albin-Simon Collin de Plancy, and is not doctrine defined by the Church. In that body of work, the figure of Beelzebub appears, for example, in the engraving by Louis Le Breton for the sixth edition of that work (1863), which describes him as "the prince of demons, the first in power and crimes after Satan."

itens.resumo: Name invoked by a man possessed by the multitude of unclean spirits that dominated him, in the Gospel episode of the Gerasene demoniac.
itens.corpo:
The three Synoptic Gospels narrate the episode of a man who lived among the tombs, in the region east of the Sea of Galilee, so dominated by unclean spirits that no one could bind him: he broke the chains and wandered among the tombs and the mountains, crying out and bruising himself with stones (Mt 8:28-34; Mk 5:1-20; Lk 8:26-39). When Jesus asks him his name, the man answers on behalf of the spirits that possessed him: "My name is Legion; for we are many" — a reference to the Roman military term. In the time of the New Testament, a legion comprised about five thousand to six thousand soldiers, organized into ten cohorts; the name, therefore, does not function as the proper name of a demon, but expresses the multitude and the organized strength of the spirits, as if they were saying: "we are many, we are united and ready to fight." The Synoptics add that the demons begged Jesus not to drive them out of the region and to allow them to enter a nearby herd of swine.

The location of the episode has given rise to a famous textual difficulty. Mark and Luke say "the country of the Gerasenes"; Matthew, "the country of the Gadarenes"; some manuscripts also have "Gergesenes." Since Gerasa (modern Jerash) lies more than fifty kilometers from the lake, and Gadara (modern Umm Qais) lies southeast of it, the ancient copyists — and later the exegetes — tried to harmonize geography and narrative, producing the variants that still divide the texts today. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his *Onomasticon* (4th century), not satisfied with the options of Gerasa and Gadara, added a third candidate: Gergesa, "a village situated beside the Lake of Tiberias, to which the swine rushed down." Local tradition and archaeology today associate the episode with Kursi, on the eastern shore of the lake, a word that some propose to be the transliteration of "Gergesa" — the geographically most plausible site, as it lies by the shore and opposite Capernaum.

At Kursi, excavations begun by chance in 1970, during road works, and conducted between 1971 and 1974 by the Israeli archaeologist Dan Urman and the Greek Vassilios Tzaferis, revealed the largest Byzantine monastic complex ever found in Israel. The monastery, dated to the fifth century (with an older chapel on a nearby hill, whose mosaic floor bore crosses, forbidden on church pavements by an imperial decree of Theodosius II from 427 onward), was surrounded by stone walls measuring 145 by 123 meters, with a watchtower, baths, a basilica church, and a stairway that descended to the lake, where pilgrims could land. The complex was destroyed in the Persian invasions of the seventh century. The traditional identification of the place with the miracle is, however, disputed: archaeologists observe that no remains from the first century were found at Kursi, which makes the direct connection with the Gospel episode uncertain.

Jesus allows the demons to leave, and they enter the swine: according to Mark 5:13, the herd numbered "about two thousand" animals, which rushed down the steep bank and were drowned in the sea. Swine were unclean animals in the Jewish tradition, and the sea represented, symbolically, chaos and the dwelling of the forces hostile to God; the scene reinforces the defeat of evil before the power of Christ. The man, healed, is later found "sitting, clothed, and in his right mind" (Mk 5:15), and asks to follow Jesus, but is sent back to proclaim to the Decapolis, a region with a Gentile majority, "how much the Lord has done for you" — one of the first missionary commissions outside the Jewish world.

The account is one of the Gospel episodes most invoked regarding Jesus' authority over evil spirits, and it already appears sculpted in a sixth-century mosaic in the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna. The name "Legion" became, in later Christian language, a common expression to designate an especially grave or multiple possession. The episode also attracted readings of a historical-political nature: the use of the term "legion," which designated the Roman occupying force, was read by some exegetes — among them the literary theorist René Girard, in "The Scapegoat" — as a symbolic cipher of the collective oppression of the time, over which Christ manifests his power.

itens.resumo: Demon in the Book of Tobit who killed Sarah's successive husbands on their wedding night, until he was driven away by the archangel Raphael; his name is associated with the Persian Aeshma Daeva, the demon of wrath.
itens.corpo:
The name Asmodeus (in Hebrew Ashmedai, in Greek Asmodaios) goes back, according to most scholars, to the Avestan aēšma-daēva, where aēšma means "wrath" and daēva, "demon" — that is, the demon of wrath in Zoroastrianism, linked to violence and the bloody sword. The compound form is not attested in Zoroastrian scripture, but it is believed to have existed, and both the Asmodaios of the Book of Tobit and the Ashmedai of Jewish tradition are thought to derive from it. This origin reflects the contact of Jewish religiosity with Persian culture in the Achaemenid period, after the exile in Babylon. An alternative etymology, now a minority view, links the name to the Hebrew root shamad, "to destroy, to annihilate."

In the Book of Tobit, a deuterocanonical text of the Old Testament (probably from the third-second centuries B.C.), Asmodeus is the main antagonist: in love with Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, he kills seven of her husbands, one after another, on the wedding night, before the marriages could be consummated, and for this reason the young woman is even accused by her maidservants of having killed her own husbands (Tobit 3:7-9). A frequently forgotten detail is that Tobias himself, in Tobit 6:15, says that the demon does not harm Sarah because he loves her — which links Asmodeus to the theme of possessive jealousy. It is later tradition, and not the biblical text, that makes him the patron of lust; the theologian Peter Binsfeld, at the end of the sixteenth century, classified him as the demon of lust among the capital vices.

When Tobias, guided by the archangel Raphael disguised as a travel companion, asks for Sarah in marriage, Raphael instructs him to burn the heart and liver of a fish caught during the journey on the Tigris River; the resulting smoke drives Asmodeus away to "upper Egypt," where Raphael himself binds and fetters him (Tobit 6:16-18; 8:2-3). Before departing, Raphael also teaches Tobias to keep prayer and a chaste marriage during the first three nights, as a remedy against evil. The episode illustrates the central theme of the book: the providence of God, who acts through angelic mediation to protect the family and restore hope amid suffering.

Outside the Bible, Asmodeus had a long literary life. The Testament of Solomon, a mystical work from the first centuries of the Christian era, rewrites the episode: it is King Solomon himself who burns the fish's liver and subdues Asmodeus, making him work on the construction of the Temple. In the Talmud, Ashmedai appears as the "king of the demons" (Pesaḥim 110a) and as the protagonist of legendary cycles in which he deceives and is deceived by Solomon; according to a midrashic tradition, he would be a son of King David, which would explain his claim to the throne. In medieval art and grimoires, Asmodeus is usually depicted with three heads — of a man, a ram, and a bull — riding a dragon. All this material belongs to literature and folklore, not to revelation: the Church acknowledges the existence of fallen angels and demons, but does not define a named hierarchy among them.
